question.prompt: Circles with centers \(P,\) \(Q,\) and \(R,\) having radii \(1,\) \(2,\) and \(3,\) respectively, lie on the same side of line \(l\) and are tangent to \(l\) at \(P',\) \(Q',\) and \(R',\) respectively, with \(Q'\) between \(P'\) and \(R'.\) The circle with center \(Q\) is externally tangent to each of the other two circles. What is the area of \(\triangle PQR?\)

solutions.explanation:
The radii to the tangent line are perpendicular to it, so the centers have heights \(1,2,3\) above \(l\). Take \(l\) as the horizontal axis, oriented so that \(P',Q',R'\) occur from left to right. We may write
\[
P=(-u,1),\qquad Q=(0,2),\qquad R=(v,3),
\]
where \(u,v>0\).

External tangency means that center distances equal sums of radii. Thus \(PQ=3\) and \(QR=5\). Their vertical differences are both \(1\), so the Pythagorean theorem gives
\[
u^2=3^2-1^2=8,\qquad v^2=5^2-1^2=24.
\]
Therefore \(u=2\sqrt2\) and \(v=2\sqrt6\).

The equally spaced center heights suggest using the midpoint \(M\) of \(PR\). Its coordinates are
\[
M=\left(\frac{v-u}{2},2\right),
\]
so \(QM\) is horizontal. Since \(v>u\),
\[
QM=\frac{v-u}{2}=\sqrt6-\sqrt2>0.
\]

Because \(M\) lies on \(PR\), segment \(QM\) divides \(\triangle PQR\) into \(\triangle PQM\) and \(\triangle RQM\). Each has base \(QM\) and height \(1\), with \(P\) and \(R\) on opposite sides of the base line. Their areas add to
\[
\frac12 QM+\frac12 QM=QM.
\]
Hence the requested area is \(\boxed{\sqrt6-\sqrt2}\), choice \(\text{D}\).
solutions.title: Use the midpoint of PR
